summary.text: An electron configuration describes how an atom's or molecule's electrons are distributed among its orbitals.
Neon's is written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, which says its 1s, 2s and 2p subshells hold two, two and six electrons.
Knowing it helps explain the periodic table, how chemical bonds hold atoms together, and the formulas and shapes of molecules.

facts.label: Subshell letters
facts.value: s, p, d and f stand for l = 0, 1, 2 and 3

facts.label: Shell capacity
facts.value: The nth shell holds up to 2n² electrons

facts.label: What decides chemistry
facts.value: The electrons in the outermost shell most determine an element's chemistry

items.prompt: A chemist describes lithium: two electrons in the lowest subshell and one in the next-higher subshell. How is its configuration written?

options.label: 1s¹ 2s²
1s² 2s¹
1s³
2s² 1s¹

items.explain: Two electrons in 1s and one in the higher-energy 2s subshell gives 1s² 2s¹.

items.prompt: Phosphorus sits in the third period. A student asks why its configuration can begin with [Ne] instead of listing every subshell.

options.label: Its inner electrons are arranged just as neon's are, so that part is shortened
Phosphorus atoms contain small clusters of real neon atoms inside them
Phosphorus has exactly as many electrons in total as neon does
The symbol is a spelling mistake that chemists have simply tolerated

items.explain: Phosphorus differs from neon only by a third shell, so the neon-like part is abbreviated as [Ne].

items.prompt: Two students write titanium's ground state as [Ar] 4s² 3d² and [Ar] 3d² 4s², and both get full marks. Why?

options.label: Only how many electrons each orbital holds matters physically, not the listing sequence
Titanium keeps switching between two different electron arrangements
The two versions describe two different atoms of titanium
The 4s and 3d orbitals turn out to be one and the same orbital

items.explain: Only the orbital occupancies have physical significance, so the order of writing is not completely fixed.

items.prompt: A student tries to place three electrons into one single orbital. Why can't this work?

options.label: Electrons repel too strongly to share any orbital at all
An orbital only holds electrons if they all point the same way
Three electrons would be too heavy for any orbital to carry
An orbital takes at most two electrons, and they must differ in spin

items.explain: Each atomic orbital admits up to two otherwise identical electrons with opposite spin.

items.prompt: A 3d subshell is completely full. How many electrons does it hold?
items.explain: A d subshell can hold ten electrons, compared with two in an s subshell and six in a p subshell.

items.prompt: A student asks why chemists happily shorten the inner part of a big atom's configuration and keep only its last few subshells in full.

options.label: Inner electrons are always identical in every element, so they never matter
Shorter notation is easier to print, and chemistry has no preference
The electrons in the outermost shell mostly decide how the element behaves
Only the last few subshells ever contain any electrons at all

items.explain: The abbreviation keeps the part that matters most: the outermost-shell electrons most determine an element's chemistry.
